lessons.title: 1. The Korean alphabet
lessons.subtitle: Hangul · who made it and why · vowels and consonants

explanations.title: Hangul
explanations.body:
Koreans use their own unique alphabet, called Hangul. It was invented by King Sejong during the Chosun Dynasty (the book dates the dynasty 1393–1910) and was known as Hun-Min-Jeong-Eum, which literally means “the correct sounds for the instruction of the people”.

Before Hangul, Koreans used Chinese characters to write. The complicated characters were hard for ordinary people to read and write properly, so ordinary people were frustrated at not being able to put their thoughts and feelings into written words. King Sejong, a revolutionary ruler and scholar, imagined a set of uniquely Korean letters that would be easy to learn, and so Hun-Min-Jeong-Eum was born.

A note on spelling: the main English dictionary spelling is “Hangul”, but following the Revised Romanization of Korean the South Korean government writes “Hangeul” in its English publications. These lessons use “Hangul”. (The book’s video about Hangul is not included.)

explanations.title: How the letters were invented: the vowels
explanations.body: Every vowel was built from one of three symbols: a dot (•) for the heavens, a horizontal stick (ㅡ) for the earth, and a vertical stick (ㅣ) for a standing person. In writing, the dot became a short stroke attached to the long stick. Look at the short strokes below.

explanations.title: How the letters were invented: the consonants
explanations.body:
The consonants copy the position and shape of the mouth, tongue and lips as the sound is made. ㄱ, which sounds like the k in kimchi or the k at the end of book, shows the side view of the tongue as you say it: freeze your tongue the moment you say “k” and its shape looks like ㄱ.

Add a strong puff of air to ㄱ and you get ㅋ. The extra stroke in ㅋ stands for that puff of air.

ㄴ, which sounds like the n in now or ban, also shows the shape of the tongue as it is said. The book also shows drawings of the lips and tongue for ㅁ, ㅅ and ㅇ; those pictures are not reproduced here.

explanations.title: 21 vowels and 19 consonants
explanations.body:
Korean writing has 21 vowels and 19 consonants. For now, just get used to the shapes; you will meet each group in the next lessons.

A diphthong is two vowel sounds joined in one gliding movement. English examples are “ye” in yes, “ya” in yarn and “ea” in steak.

ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ and ㅉ are called double consonants, glottal consonants or tensed consonants.

lessons.title: 2. Syllable blocks
lessons.subtitle: (C)V(C) · vertical and horizontal sticks · the placeholder ㅇ

explanations.title: A syllable is a block
explanations.body:
Syllables are the building blocks of words. The word kimchi has two syllables: kim and chi. In Korean a syllable has one optional initial consonant, a vowel, and one optional final consonant: (C)V(C). That gives four shapes of spoken syllable:

1. V: a vowel
2. CV: a consonant and a vowel
3. VC: a vowel and a consonant
4. CVC: a consonant, a vowel and a consonant

In writing, every syllable is fitted into an imaginary square block, for looks and for the sake of calligraphy.

explanations.title: Where the letters go in the block
explanations.body:
The initial consonant goes to the left of a vertical-stick vowel (ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ), or on top of a horizontal-stick vowel (ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ). In 가 the ㄱ stands to the left of ㅏ because ㅏ is a vertical stick; in 그 the ㄱ sits on top of ㅡ because ㅡ is a horizontal stick.

A final consonant always goes at the bottom of the block: 샘 (ㅅ + ㅐ + ㅁ) and 놀 (ㄴ + ㅗ + ㄹ).

explanations.title: The placeholder ㅇ
explanations.body: When a syllable has no initial consonant (V or VC), a placeholder ㅇ is written in its place, again only for looks. At the start of a syllable ㅇ has no sound of its own, so 오 and 이 sound exactly like ㅗ and ㅣ.

lessons.title: 4. Consonants ㄱ and ㄴ
lessons.subtitle: 기역 · 니은 · 가 거 고 구 그 기 · 나 너 노 누 느 니

explanations.title: ㄱ (기역)
explanations.body:
ㄱ is named 기역 and is said in two ways.

1. At the beginning of a word it has a k-like sound. The first ㄱ in 고기 (meat) is like the “c” in cool or the “k” in kiss, but, unlike the English c or k, it is not followed by a heavy puff of air.
2. Between vowels it has a g-like sound. The second ㄱ in 고기 is like the “g” in go or good.

ㄱ changes its shape a little for looks, depending on whether the vowel is a vertical or a horizontal stick; compare 가 and 그.

explanations.title: ㄴ (니은)
explanations.body: ㄴ is named 니은 and is said like the “n” in nice or no.

lessons.title: 5. Consonants ㄷ and ㄹ
lessons.subtitle: 디귿 · 리을 · 다 더 도 두 드 디 · 라 러 로 루 르 리

explanations.title: ㄷ (디귿)
explanations.body:
ㄷ is named 디귿 and is said in two ways.

1. At the beginning of a word it has a t-like sound. The ㄷ in 다리 (leg; bridge) is like the “t” in tall and team, but, unlike the English t, it is not followed by a heavy puff of air.
2. Between vowels, or between some voiced consonants, it has a d-like sound. The ㄷ in 구두 (shoes) is like the “d” in do or day.

explanations.title: ㄹ (리을)
explanations.body:
ㄹ is named 리을 and is said in two ways.

1. At the beginning of a word, or at the end of a syllable, it has an l-like sound: the ㄹ in 라면 (ramen noodles) and 발 (foot) is like the “l” in lady or long. The tip of the tongue touches the palate, not the back of the teeth.
2. Between vowels it is a “flap”: the ㄹ in 나라 (nation) or 도로 (street; road) sounds something like the “t” in water or the “tt” in latter.

A flap is made with a single quick contraction of the muscles, so that the tongue is thrown against the roof of the mouth. The “t” in batter or quarter is a flap when an unstressed vowel follows it.

exercises.explanation: Between vowels ㄹ is a flap, similar to the t in water.

exercises.prompt: Where does the tip of the tongue touch when you say the l-like ㄹ?
exercises.explanation: For ㄹ the tongue tip touches the palate, not the back of the teeth.

explanations.title: Greeting and introducing yourself
explanations.body: These are the first six expressions of the course. Practice them aloud, then use them with a partner. The book’s example answers are 김민수입니다 (the name of the person speaking is Kim Minsoo) and 시카고입니다 or 서울입니다 for the hometown. In a real conversation you replace the name and the place with your own, followed by 입니다. The book explains the grammar in later lessons.

lessons.title: 9. Two more simple vowels: ㅐ and ㅔ

explanations.title: ㅐ and ㅔ
explanations.body:
In Lesson 1 you learned six of the eight simple vowels. The last two are ㅐ and ㅔ.

ㅐ is made up of ㅏ and ㅣ. It sounds like the “a” in apple or sad.
ㅔ is made up of ㅓ and ㅣ. It sounds like the “e” in bed or elk.

Unlike English, the difference in sound between ㅐ and ㅔ is not clear: the two sound very much alike, so you will learn which one a word uses by learning the word itself.

lessons.title: 10. Y-vowels: ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ
lessons.subtitle: 야 여 요 유 · 갸 겨 교 규

explanations.title: Six y-vowels
explanations.body:
Korean has six y-vowels: ㅑ, ㅕ, ㅛ, ㅠ, ㅒ and ㅖ. They are called y-vowels because each sounds like a vowel preceded by a y, as in young, yodel, you, yell. In writing, the two dots, or two small sticks, stand for that y sound.

explanations.title: Six w-vowels
explanations.body:
Korean has six w-vowels: ㅘ, ㅝ, ㅚ, ㅟ, ㅙ and ㅞ. They are called w-vowels because they begin with an English w sound, as in watt, win, week, wet, world. In writing, a w-vowel is ㅗ or ㅜ combined with ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ, ㅐ or ㅔ: ㅘ, ㅝ, ㅚ, ㅟ, ㅙ, ㅞ.

To say one, sound the two vowels quickly one after the other, as if they were one sound. Say ㅗ and ㅏ quickly and you say 와. This lesson has the first four; ㅙ and ㅞ come in Lesson 4.

explanations.title: ㅢ
explanations.body:
ㅢ is made up of ㅡ and ㅣ. Saying the two quickly together gives a sound that, unfortunately, has no English equivalent.

When ㅢ comes after any consonant other than the placeholder ㅇ (as in 늬 or 희), it loses the ㅡ sound: 늬 sounds the same as 니, and 희 sounds the same as 히. Only when it starts the syllable on its own, as in 의, do you hear the full ㅡ + ㅣ sound.

A note on romanization (mine): the Revised Romanization always writes ㅢ as ui, even where it is said like ㅣ, so 희 is romanized hui although it sounds like 히.

explanations.title: Plain and aspirated
explanations.body:

To practise, hold a piece of paper in front of your mouth. If the paper moves, you have said the aspirated sound correctly; if it does not, you have said the plain counterpart (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ or ㅈ).

lessons.title: 23. Two more y-vowels: ㅒ ㅖ
lessons.subtitle: 얘 · 걔 · 쟤 · 예 · 계 · 폐

explanations.title: ㅒ and ㅖ
explanations.body:
You already know four y-vowels (ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ). Lesson 4 adds the other two, ㅒ and ㅖ.

ㅒ sounds like the “ya” in yank. You make it by adding a y sound to 애.

ㅖ sounds like the “ye” in yes. You make it by adding a y sound to 에.

Unlike the other y-vowels, ㅒ loses its y sound when it comes after any consonant other than ㅅ: 걔 sounds the same as 개, and 쟤 sounds the same as 재. ㅖ loses its y sound after a consonant too: 계 sounds the same as 게, and 폐 sounds the same as 페. As with ㅐ and ㅔ, it is hard to tell ㅒ and ㅖ apart.

Note: 섀 appears only in a loanword such as 섀도 마스크 (shadow mask), so it sounds like the “sha” in shadow.

rows: the same as 헤 (by the same rule)

explanations.title: Spelling and sound (mine)
explanations.body: The Revised Romanization spells ㅒ and ㅖ with the y even where it is not said, the same way it spells 희 as hui although it is said 히. So 걔 is written gyae and 계 is written gye, but they are said like 개 and 게. With the placeholder ㅇ (얘, 예) the y is kept. After ㅈ the romanization drops the y (쟤 is jae), as it does for 져 (jeo).

explanations.title: Plain, aspirated and double
explanations.body:
ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ and ㅉ are called “double” consonants because they are spelled by doubling ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ and ㅈ. They are also known as “glottal” or “tensed” consonants, because they are produced by holding the throat tense and then releasing the sound without a puff of air.

ㄲ, ㄸ and ㅃ are similar to “k”, “t” and “p” when they immediately follow the consonant “s”, as in sky, star and spy. ㅆ is similar to the “s” sound followed by a stressed vowel, as in sun, soul and silly. The double consonants are easier to understand beside their counterparts.

explanations.title: Looking up a word
explanations.body: To find “tourist” in an English dictionary you look for t, then o, u, r, i, s, t. Korean works the same way. To look up 가다 you use ㄱ, ㅏ, ㄷ, ㅏ (four steps); to look up 입다 you use ㅇ, ㅣ, ㅂ, ㄷ, ㅏ (five steps, because 입 has a final consonant).

explanations.title: The consonant sequence
explanations.body: The Korean dictionary is organised by consonants. The main sections come in this order: ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ ㅈ ㅊ ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅎ. The double consonants are at the end of their own sections, so if you are looking up ㄲ you find it at the very end of the ㄱ section.

explanations.title: The vowel sequence
explanations.body: After the initial consonant, use the vowel sequence. The y-vowels and w-vowels are slotted in beside the vowels they are built on: ㅐ after ㅏ, ㅒ after ㅑ, ㅔ after ㅓ, ㅖ after ㅕ, ㅘ ㅙ ㅚ after ㅗ, ㅝ ㅞ ㅟ after ㅜ, and ㅢ after ㅡ.

explanations.body:

In the part for the syllable 가, use the consonant sequence to find the first consonant of the next syllable (ㄷ). 4. In the words that begin with 가ㄷ, use the vowel sequence to find the vowel (ㅏ).

A note (mine): a syllable with no final consonant comes before the same syllable with one, so 가 comes before 간. The book’s activities do not need this, but a real dictionary does.

lessons.title: 30. Loanword rules
lessons.subtitle: 스트라이크 · 뉴욕 · 커피숍 · 파리 · 라디오 · 필름

explanations.title: Spelling English words in Korean
explanations.body: In the past several decades, numerous English words have become part of everyday Korean. That does not make them easy for a native English speaker to recognise, because Koreans spell and pronounce loanwords differently. For example, the one-syllable English word “strike” is spelled 스트라이크, a word of five syllables. These rules of thumb help you recognise loanwords as you learn Korean.

explanations.title: 1. Diphthongs are two vowels
explanations.body: A diphthong is treated as two separate vowel sounds. The exception is the diphthong /ou/ as in boat and note, which becomes one vowel, 오.

explanations.title: 2. A loose consonant gets ㅡ
explanations.body: In Korean a consonant or a vowel cannot stand alone as a syllable. A consonant has to depend on a vowel, directly before or after it. So an extra vowel (ㅡ) is inserted next to any loose consonant or cluster of consonants: s-t-r-aik becomes 스-트-라이-크.

explanations.title: 3. Final consonants: only ㄱ ㄴ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ
explanations.body: Only ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ and ㅇ can be used at the end of a syllable. So the sounds “k”, “p” and “t” after a vowel in a syllable are spelled ㄱ, ㅂ and ㅅ. The “k” in New York is spelled ㄱ, not ㅋ (뉴욕); the “p” in coffee shop is spelled ㅂ, not ㅍ (커피숍).

explanations.title: 4. No double consonants at the start
explanations.body: The double consonants ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ are not used at the start of a syllable in a loanword, even when the word has a sound like ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ or ㅉ. The “P” of Paris is spelled with ㅍ: 파리 (not 빠리).

explanations.title: 5. r and l are both ㄹ
explanations.body: In Korean “r” and “l” are considered the same sound and are both spelled ㄹ. However, an “r” after a vowel, as in card or computer, is silent. When an “l” has a consonant before or after it, as in slide and film, it is often spelled ㄹㄹ.

explanations.title: 6. Vowels that need attention
explanations.body: The “a” of California is associated with ㅐ and the “e” of Minnesota with ㅔ. Because of the influence of British English, “o” tends to be associated with ㅗ.

explanations.title: 7. Sounds Korean does not have
explanations.body: Sounds that do not exist in Korean are approximated by the closest Korean sounds. The “th” of theme or Thatcher becomes ㅅ, ㅌ or ㄷ. The “f” of film and file becomes ㅍ or ㅎ; fitness can be 피트니스 or 휘트니스.

explanations.title: 8. Loanwords from other languages
explanations.body: For loanwords that come from other languages, the local pronunciation is reflected: Paris (French) is 파리, and arbeit (German, “part-time work”) is 아르바이트.

exercises.explanation: The “th” of theme and Thatcher becomes ㅅ, ㅌ or ㄷ: 테마, 대처.

exercises.explanation: The “f” of film and file becomes ㅍ or ㅎ: 필름, 파일, 휘트니스.

lessons.title: 35. Final consonants: only seven sounds

explanations.title: Consonants at the end of a syllable
explanations.body:
So far you have met the 14 basic consonants and 5 double consonants as initial consonants, the ones that come at the beginning of a syllable. With the exception of ㄸ, ㅃ and ㅉ, all of them can also be used as final consonants (batchim), written under the vowel. For example:

악 안 앋 알 암 압 앗 앙 앚 앛 앜 앝 앞 앟 앆 았

In speech, however, only seven final consonants keep their sound value: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ and ㅇ. All the others merge into three of these seven sounds.

rows: ㄷ, ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ, ㅎ

headers: Romanization at the end of a syllable

explanations.title: Same place in the mouth
explanations.body: The merging consonants use similar places of articulation. For example, ㄱ, ㄲ and ㅋ are all velar consonants, that is, consonants made with the back of the tongue against the soft palate, so they all end up as the same ㄱ sound.

explanations.title: A note on romanization (mine)
explanations.body: The Revised Romanization writes the sound that is actually said: a final ㄱ, ㄲ or ㅋ is k; a final ㄷ, ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ or ㅎ is t; a final ㅂ or ㅍ is p; a final ㄹ is l; and a final ㅇ is ng. So 앞 is ap and 앟 is at.

explanations.title: The /k/ group: ㄱ, ㄲ, ㅋ

explanations.title: The /p/ group: ㅂ, ㅍ

explanations.title: Two number systems
explanations.body: There are two number systems in Korean: Sino-Korean numbers and native (or pure) Korean numbers. Sino-Korean refers to the set of numbers that originated from, or were influenced by, the Chinese language. This lesson has the Sino-Korean numbers; the native numbers are introduced in a later lesson (Lesson 6).

explanations.title: Building the other numbers
explanations.body:
In this numbering system, 45 is considered as 4 × 10 + 5, so 45 reads 사십오. All other two-digit numbers read in this way: 21 is 2 × 10 + 1, 이십일; 99 is 구십구.

A note (mine): for 10 to 19 you say just 십, 십일, 십이…, with no 일 before 십; 17 is 십칠, not 일십칠. Some of the sound changes you learned apply too: 십 plus 일 is said 시빌, 십 plus 육 is said 심뉵 (16), and 십 plus 구 is said 십꾸.

explanations.title: Carried over, in English and in Korean
explanations.body:
Say these English phrases at normal speed: “Stop it!” and “She baked it.” They sound like “Sto pit” and “She bake dit”. This is because the “p” in stop and the “d” in baked are “carried over” to the word it. The same thing happens in Korean.

Whenever a syllable ends in a consonant and the next syllable starts with a vowel, the final consonant is carried over to the next syllable. This is known as the sound-linking rule, or the consonant carry-over rule. In the book’s picture, the ㄴ at the end of the first syllable of 단어 moves to the second syllable, so the word sounds like 다너. (The picture is not reproduced; the English for 단어 is mine.)

explanations.title: Reading the pronunciation
explanations.body: The Revised Romanization follows what is said, so it shows the carried consonant at the start of the next syllable: 군인 is gunin and 한국어 is hangugeo. A note (mine): a final ㅇ (ng) is never carried over, so a word such as 송아지 (songaji) is said as it is written.

lessons.title: 45. Final consonant clusters

explanations.title: Eleven clusters, one sound
explanations.body: There are 11 consonant clusters that come at the end of a syllable: ㄳ, ㄵ, ㄶ, ㄺ, ㄻ, ㄼ, ㄽ, ㄾ, ㄿ, ㅀ and ㅄ. Although these clusters are made up of two different consonants, they have only one sound value. In other words, one of the consonants is silent. The next tables show which one. In this lesson you practise ㄵ, ㄶ, ㄺ, ㄻ, ㄼ, ㅀ and ㅄ; syllables that end in the other clusters are practised later in the course. (The one example for each cluster is taken from the book’s tables.)

explanations.title: The second consonant is silent
explanations.body: In ㄳ, ㄵ, ㄶ, ㄼ, ㄽ, ㄾ, ㅀ and ㅄ, the second consonant is silent. The book prints these examples with the sound between slashes (the meanings are not given).

explanations.title: The first consonant is silent
explanations.body: In ㄺ, ㄻ and ㄿ, the first consonant is silent. The book prints 읊 as /읖/; since a final ㅍ is said ㅂ, the table below writes the sound as 읍.

explanations.title: Exceptions
explanations.body: There are a few exceptions to the rules above. In the case of 밟, as in 밟다 (to tread), the ㄹ is silent: 밟 is said 밥. And when ㄺ is part of a verb and it is followed by the consonant ㄱ, the ㄱ is silent: 맑게 is said 말께 and 밝게 is said 발께. (The meanings of 맑게 and 밝게 are mine.)

explanations.title: The native numbers
explanations.body: Below are the native (or pure) Korean numbers. Unlike the Sino-Korean system, 20, 30, 40 and so forth have unique names. Therefore 46 is considered 40 + 6 and reads 마흔여섯. Listen to the numbers and repeat them aloud several times. (The recording is not included.)

explanations.title: Building the other numbers
explanations.body: As in the Sino-Korean system, the other numbers are the ten plus the one: 46 is 40 + 6 = 마흔여섯; 99 is 90 + 9 = 아흔아홉. A note (mine): for 11, 12 … say 열하나, 열둘 …, and for 21, 22 … say 스물하나, 스물둘 …. The book stops at 99, and its native numbers have no word for 100.

explanations.title: Sound changes in some numbers (mine)
explanations.body: The book teaches only how the numbers are built. In speech, an ㄴ or ㄹ is added when a ten is followed by 여섯, 일곱 or 여덟: 열여섯 is said 열려섣, 서른일곱 is said 서른닐곱. The romanization follows what is said. With 아홉 the consonant is carried over, as in Lesson 6: 열아홉 is said 여라홉.

explanations.title: Two number systems side by side
explanations.body: Compare the two systems for the same number. Which one to use depends on what you are counting; the book introduces that later.

lessons.title: 51. Assimilation: three directions
lessons.subtitle: 앞문 → 암문 · 칼날 → 칼랄 · 백로 → 뱅노

explanations.title: Salient Korean phonological rules
explanations.body: The Appendix covers several salient Korean phonological rules that Korean language learners must be familiar with. Understanding the rules will help you not only to pronounce Korean more naturally but also to understand, with less effort, what Koreans say.

explanations.title: What assimilation is
explanations.body: Assimilation is a sound change due to the influence of an adjoining sound. It is a universal phenomenon. In Korean, assimilation occurs in consonants when a “dominant” consonant adjoins another consonant. Assimilation occurs in three different directions: backward, forward and reciprocal.

explanations.title: Backward, forward, reciprocal
explanations.body: Backward assimilation: being influenced by a following consonant, the preceding consonant is assimilated. Forward assimilation: being influenced by a preceding consonant, the following consonant is assimilated. Reciprocal assimilation: two neighboring consonants are assimilated because of their mutual influence. The book shows one word for each in a picture, with the changed sounds marked.

explanations.title: Three categories
explanations.body: Depending on the type of sound change, we can place assimilation into three categories: (1) nasalization, (2) ㄴ to ㄹ assimilation, and (3) assimilation of the “stop sound” before ㄹ. The next lessons take them in turn, followed by the other sound changes of the Appendix.

explanations.title: Nasal consonants are powerful
explanations.body: ㄴ, ㅁ and ㅇ are nasal consonants, which are powerful “sound change agents.” (Nasal consonants are produced while the velum, or soft palate, is lowered so that some air escapes through the nose.) Whenever a stop sound like ㄱ, ㄷ or ㅂ precedes one of these nasal consonants, it is nasalized into ㅇ, ㄴ or ㅁ. (A stop sound is characterized by the momentary blocking of some part of the oral cavity; ㄱ, ㄷ and ㅂ are typical stop sounds.) Also note that ㄹ is nasalized to ㄴ when it is preceded by a nasal consonant.

(The book gives no English; none is added.)

explanations.title: ㄴ to ㄹ assimilation
explanations.body: When ㄴ comes before or after ㄹ, the ㄴ sound changes into the ㄹ sound because of the influence of the consonant ㄹ, as in 신라 (said 실라) and 칼날 (said 칼랄). Say each word and repeat it several times. (The recording is not included.)

explanations.title: The stop sound before ㄹ
explanations.body: When a stop consonant such as ㄱ, ㄷ or ㅂ comes before ㄹ, the stop sound is nasalized into ㅇ, ㄴ or ㅁ. Then the ㄹ sound is in turn also nasalized because of the influence of the new nasalized sound. So the change takes two steps, which the book prints for each word. explanations.title: Tense after another consonant
explanations.body: In English, we pronounce k, p and t more tensely when they are preceded by s, as in stop, sky and spy. We can observe a similar phenomenon in Korean. The consonants ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ and ㅈ become ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ and ㅉ, respectively, when they follow another stop, a nasal sound, or ㄹ. Say each word and repeat it several times. (The recording is not included.) The Revised Romanization does not show this change: 학교 is hakgyo. (The column “after” is mine.)

explanations.title: Exceptions
explanations.body: There are several exceptions to the tensification rule, as shown in 월부, 팔고, 단발 and 헌병. The book gives only the audio for them; a note (mine): in these words the consonant after ㄹ or ㄴ is not tensified, so the words are said as they are written.

explanations.title: The spelling you cannot see (mine)
explanations.body: Many words are written with a plain consonant but said with a tense one, so the tense sound is not in the spelling. When you read, remember that ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ and ㅈ after a final stop are tense, as in 학교 (학꾜).

lessons.title: 57. Palatalization

explanations.title: Tongue toward the roof of the mouth
explanations.body:
Say tree and table, and division and song. Do you notice that t in tree is pronounced differently from t in table, and that s in division is pronounced differently from s in song? That is because the t in tree and the s in division are palatalized: they are produced with the blade (or front) of the tongue drawn up more toward the roof of the mouth than in normal pronunciation. We call this palatalization.

When a syllable-final consonant ㄷ or ㅌ is followed by the vowel ㅣ or the “y” vowels, ㄷ and ㅌ are pronounced ㅈ and ㅊ, respectively. Say each word and repeat it several times. (The recording is not included.) The book prints 닫혀요 in two steps: /다텨요/ (ㄷ + ㅎ make ㅌ) and then /다쳐요/.

lessons.title: 58. Korean vocabulary: three components
lessons.subtitle: Sino-Korean · native · loanwords

explanations.title: Three components
explanations.body: Korean vocabulary is composed of three components: Sino-Korean words (approximately 60%), native Korean words (approximately 35%) and loanwords (approximately 5%).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean words
explanations.body: Sino- means “China” or “Chinese.” Sino-Korean vocabulary refers to a set of words that originated from, or were influenced by, the Chinese literary (written traditional) language. Sino-Korean words are easy to identify in the dictionary because they are always followed by their Chinese characters. Examples of dictionary entries:

rows: a term; a session; a semester

explanations.title: Learn the building blocks
explanations.body: Although you are not required to learn Chinese characters in the Korean Basic Course, it is important to know the meanings of the individual Sino-Korean components, because they serve as building blocks for numerous Sino-Korean words. Take the character 學 (학): it means learning or school, and is part of the following words, which all have to do with learning or school.

explanations.title: Native Korean words
explanations.body: Native Korean words are the underlying words of everyday language: food, clothing, shelter, locations, basic actions, activities and states, lower-level numerals, anatomy, natural objects, animals and so on. Thousands of sound-symbolic (onomatopoeic and mimetic) words, idioms, proverbs, and most of the grammatical markers and affixes are native Korean words. They are also easy to identify in the dictionary, because they are not followed by Chinese characters. Examples of dictionary entries (the book adds short Korean notes in brackets, [환상] for 꿈 and [꿈 같은 상태] for 꿈결, meaning “illusion” and “a dream-like state”):

a dream-like state; a dreamy (ecstatic) state of mind

explanations.title: English loanwords
explanations.body: There are over 20,000 loanwords in Korean and, fortunately, most of them (approximately 90%) are from English. Examples of English loanwords in the dictionary:

lessons.title: 59. Two types of verbs
lessons.subtitle: 가다 · 먹다 · 좋다 · 슬프다 · action and stative

explanations.title: Verbs in dictionary form
explanations.body: Verbs are not only one of the key sentence elements but also, arguably, the most crucial part of speech in mastering Korean. Verbs found in the dictionary always end in 다, as in 가다 (to go; to proceed) and 먹다 (to eat). They are called “verbs in dictionary form.” Much like infinitives in English, Korean verbs are conjugated for use in a given sentence. (You learn to conjugate them in the chapters that follow this unit.)

explanations.title: Action verbs and stative verbs
explanations.body: There are two major types of verbs in Korean: action verbs and stative verbs (also known as descriptive verbs). Action verbs are those typically treated as verbs in English, and stative verbs are typically treated as adjectives in English.

rows: to be tall; to be big
tables.title: Stative verbs (SV)

explanations.title: Why the difference matters
explanations.body: Stative verbs are like English adjectives in meaning, except that they are translated as “to be …”. The distinction between the two types is crucial for your mastery of Korean, because stative verbs behave slightly differently from action verbs when they are conjugated. It is also important to keep in mind that stative verbs are not true adjectives: they cannot be placed before a modified noun unless they go through some “cosmetic changes.” In other words, to use them like English adjectives, we have to turn them into “attributive forms.” You learn how to make attributive forms later in the course.
